question: On CSF Gram stain from a 22-year-old with purulent meningitis, you observe lancet-shaped Gram-positive diplococci. Which organism is most likely, and what is the treatment of choice?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: N. meningitidis appears as Gram-NEGATIVE kidney-shaped (bean-shaped) diplococci, often seen intracellularly within neutrophils. The Gram-positive, lancet-shaped morphology described here is inconsistent with Neisseria.

Lancet-shaped (flame-shaped) Gram-positive diplococci are pathognomonic of S. pneumoniae. Treatment is ceftriaxone (or benzyl penicillin if susceptible) plus adjunctive dexamethasone to reduce inflammation and prevent neurological sequelae such as sensorineural deafness.

Listeria appears as Gram-positive RODS (bacilli), not diplococci. It characteristically causes meningitis in neonates, the elderly, and immunocompromised patients. Lancet-shaped diplococci are specific to pneumococcus.

H. influenzae appears as small Gram-NEGATIVE coccobacilli (pleomorphic short rods), not Gram-positive diplococci. It was formerly common in unvaccinated children but is now rare due to Hib vaccination.

overallFeedback.feedback: Focus on two features: Gram reaction (positive vs. negative) and morphology (diplococci vs. rods vs. coccobacilli). Lancet-shaped Gram-positive diplococci = S. pneumoniae; kidney-shaped Gram-negative diplococci = N. meningitidis.
Well done! Recognising organism-specific morphology on Gram stain — lancet-shaped Gram-positive diplococci for pneumococcus — enables immediate targeted therapy and improves patient outcomes.
